old_entry.title: Tengai Makyō: Ziria
old_entry.subtitle: Ziria Shows What Changes When an RPG Moves to CD
old_entry.summary: On June 30, 1989 Hudson Soft released Tengai Makyō: Ziria for the PC Engine CD-ROM².
body: On June 30, 1989 Hudson Soft released Tengai Makyō: Ziria for the PC Engine CD-ROM². Red Company's role-playing game used optical storage not simply to hold more data, but to make room for voices, music and audiovisual presentation on a scale unusual for the period. Its imaginary Japan, called Jipang, mixes folklore and caricature. Ziria is therefore an early document of how the CD could change the tone, pacing and production ambition of a console RPG.

The first game Tengai Makyō: Ziria (1989), released for the PC Engine CD-ROM² system, was notable as the first RPG released on CD-ROM and the first in the genre to feature animated cut scenes and voice acting. The plot and characters were inspired by the Japanese folk tale Jiraiya Goketsu Monogatari (with the protagonist's name deliberately misspelled, per the fantastic theme).

The main series is composed of three separate games within the land of 'Jipang' (a fictional feudal Japan using the name given by Italian merchant Marco Polo), each follows a descendant of the 'Fire Clan' and supporting cast in battles against a range of often comical villains. The stories of the games, though primarily of 'fantasy' fare, are inspired by and a parody of misconceptions about Japanese culture by Western societies.

The series is purported to be based on a book entitled "Far East of Eden" written by a Paul Hieronymus Chada (typically written as P.H. Chada), who is presented as a 19th-century Smithsonian professor of oriental studies. The book and P.H. Chada do not exist, and 'P.H. Chada' is actually derived from 'Prince (Oji) Hiroi'. This is part of how the setting is supposed based on the misconceptions Western societies held with regard to Japan in the past. The person "Hiroshi Adachi" credited as creating the series is also fictional, with the roles he is credited for actually being performed by Hiroi. "Adachi"/"Chada" also had a personal website which was actually run by Hiroi.

original.old_heading: The CD is more than extra space
original.old_body: The CD-ROM² format lets Hudson and Red Company use recorded voices, music and presented sequences with a richness difficult to achieve on ordinary HuCards, turning the medium itself into part of the spectacle. The choice needs to be read within the technical and production constraints of its period. Memory, processors, storage, peripherals and pipelines are not neutral background details: they define what can be shown and therefore what can become interaction. A project gains identity when it turns a limitation or capability of the hardware into a recognizable rule. Technology matters here less as a specification list than as a method, making visible the passage from an available tool to a form of play that would previously have been harder to build.

source_paragraphs: The first game Tengai Makyō: Ziria (1989), released for the PC Engine CD-ROM² system, was notable as the first RPG released on CD-ROM and the first in the genre to feature animated cut scenes and voice acting. The plot and characters were inspired by the Japanese folk tale Jiraiya Goketsu Monogatari (with the protagonist's name deliberately misspelled, per the fantastic theme). The music for the game was also composed by the Academy Award winning musician Ryuichi Sakamoto. The game was previewed in the November 1990 issue of Computer Gaming World. The writer Roe R. Adams (also a co-developer for the Wizardry games) described it as "a truly gigantic game" that "seems to be about the size of 2 or 3 Ultimas put together." He suggested that, if "NEC can handle the mammoth translating job, Ziria could be the game hit of 1991" unless, "of course, Nintendo counters with Zelda III or Dragon Warrior III, and Sega with Phantasy Star III."

original.old_heading: Jipang reinvents Japan as a stage
original.old_body: Ziria sets its adventure in Jipang, a fantastical and deliberately distorted version of Japan that combines folkloric figures, humor and role-playing conventions. Writing does not remain separate from the rules. Goals, characters and transformations gain weight because players encounter them through actions, constraints and consequences, not only during narrative scenes. Story organizes the experience while the system gives the story concrete form. It is a difficult balance: when it works, a plot development also changes how a battle, a space or a choice is read. The work's memory then grows from the connection between what is told and what the player is asked to do.
